prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Clobber game on a 5x6 grid. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: list[int], opponent: list[int]) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - Board size is 5 rows x 6 columns. - `you` and `opponent` are 5x6 arrays describing the board. - Values are 0 or 1. - `you[row, col] == 1` means you have a piece at cell `(row, col)`. - `opponent[row, col] == 1` means the opponent has a piece at cell `(row, col)`. - For any `(row, col)`, at most one of `you[row, col]` and `opponent[row, col]` is 1. # Action / Return Format - Return a string move in the format `'row,col,dir'`. - `row` is the row of the starting cell (0-4). - `col` is the column of the starting cell (0-5). - `dir` is the direction of the move: `'U'` (up), `'R'` (right), `'D'` (down), `'L'` (left). - The start cell must contain your piece. - The destination cell must be in bounds and contain an opponent piece. - A legal move must capture an adjacent opponent piece by moving one square orthogonally onto it. - The opponent piece is removed; your piece occupies the destination square; your starting square becomes empty. - The first player to have no legal moves on their turn loses. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm approaching this Clobber game problem by using iterative deepening alpha-beta search, since a full analysis of the 5x6 board is computationally infeasible. The key insight is that mobility—the number of available moves—matters far more than piece count, since a player who runs out of legal moves loses the game.

I'm implementing a negamax algorithm with alpha-beta pruning and a time constraint. To optimize for speed on the 30-cell board, I'm switching from numpy arrays to bitboards, where each player's pieces are represented as a 30-bit integer. This lets me compute moves efficiently by checking bit positions and using bitwise operations for directional shifts—moving up subtracts 6, down adds 6, left subtracts 1, and right adds 1—with boundary masks to prevent wrapping.

Implementing bitboard move generation... Building the move generator...

Now I'm implementing negamax with alpha-beta pruning to evaluate positions, where I return a loss if there are no legal moves, use mobility difference as the heuristic at depth zero, and recursively search deeper positions by applying each move and swapping perspectives.

Finalizing the policy function... I'm reconsidering the scoring system for terminal nodes—when a player has no moves, they lose, so I need to return a large negative value. The key insight is that I want to prefer delaying losses, so shorter paths to losing should be penalized more heavily than longer ones. I'll use a formula like returning negative infinity adjusted by the remaining depth, so the negamax algorithm naturally prefers moves that extend the game longer before inevitable defeat.

Implementing negamax with terminal scoring... Writing the game logic... Finishing the move selection loop and validating the bitmask logic for detecting adjacent pieces, particularly checking that the left shift doesn't wrap around incorrectly at column boundaries. The starting position for Clobber has alternating colors like a checkerboard with all 30 cells filled initially, but the search will handle that without special casing. I'm going to be more conservative with the time limit and set it to 0.8 seconds instead of 0.85 to account for Python's overhead, though the time checks happen frequently enough at each negamax node that it should still be responsive.
